1) Fee-for-service (FFS) lifestyle medicine practice within a large health system

a) In recent decades, large health systems have become the dominant healthcare providers in
communities, providing an efficient means for healthcare delivery and reaching a broad patient base.

b) Running a lifestyle medicine practice within this model has many advantages, including ability
to collect insurance, no membership fees (as compared to direct primary care [DPC] and private
practice models), ability to serve a variety of populations, access to network of specialists and allied
health providers, and low barrier to entry for providers.

¢) There are also disadvantages, including less autonomy for providers, a need to work within corporate
constraints, and reimbursement largely based on volume, which encourages shorter visits.**°

2) DPC lifestyle medicine clinic****

a) In this model, patients typically pay a membership fee for access to a healthcare provider and
in most cases, additional lifestyle-based services (e.g., fitness classes, cooking classes, access
to health coach, etc.). Providers may choose what services to offer based on what may be most
needed in their communities. By moving outside of the administrative burdens of the traditional
insurance-based billing system, these practices are able to provide a wide spectrum of care in a
transparent and affordable manner, while allowing providers more autonomy and patients better
access to lifestyle medicine services.

3) Concierge medicine**?“**

a) Like a DPC practice, concierge medicine is membership-based and offers patients faster access to
providers through in-person or remote care. Appointment times are typically longer than in the FFS
model. Unlike DPC practices, concierge practices charge insurance companies for office visits, in
addition to charging a membership fee to individuals. This allows physicians to have two forms of
revenue, while allowing patients better access to providers and additional lifestyle-based services,
as with DPC. Advantages to this model are similar to those of a DPC clinic.

C-peptide: a stimulated C-peptide measurement may be used to assess endogenous insulin production to

system in chronic disease care. The model, developed by Ed Wagner, MD, centers on an informed,
activated, and engaged patient and a prepared, proactive practice team.

Drop-in group medical appointments (DIGMAs): are used for many types of medical diseases. With
these appointments, patients can walk-in and be seen in a group.

Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle: a method for creating change that includes planning, doing,
studying, and acting on each incremental change. The method often involves several cycles of small-scale
improvements.

Root cause analysis: this tool is used when something goes wrong, or when a “near-miss” is experienced.
Root cause analysis involves repeatedly asking, “Why?” to get to the root cause of an incident and then
asking, “So what?” to determine the consequence of what occurred and to help reframe what's important.

Shared medical appointments (SMAs): also known as a group visit, SMAs occur when multiple patients
are seen as a group for follow-up care or management of chronic conditions.
